effects.original_title: Default neglect in attempts at social influence
effects.original_authors: Zlatev, J. J.; Daniels, D. P.; Kim, H.; Neale, M. A.
effects.original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
effects.outcome: Percentage of choice architects selecting the optimal default (vs. 50% chance) for the same job scenario, presented as a simplified automatic-assignment choice without the default-framing confound
effects.contrast: observed optimal-default selection rate vs. 50% chance
effects.description: In Zlatev et al.'s (2017) Study 1h, choice architects trying to steer a new employee toward a target job selected the optimal default significantly less often than chance (default neglect).
effects.citation_sentence: To directly examine whether default neglect depends on the complexity of the experimental materials, Experiment 2 includes both a direct and a conceptual replication of Zlatev et al.'s (2017) Study 1h.
effects.evidence: Experiment 2 Results and discussion (p. 699): "In our conceptual replication, however, we found the opposite pattern. In contrast to the original results, ... Overall, participants chose the optimal default 61.5% of the time, which was significantly greater than chance, χ2(1, N = 265) = 13.59, p < .001"; Abstract: "our conceptual replication, which simplified the task, instead found the opposite."
effects.notes: Authors label it a conceptual replication (same job context and trade-offs, but advice-giving removed and the choice is an explicit automatic assignment). Significantly above chance in both target conditions (59.8%, p = .03; 63.2%, p = .003) and pooled; authors explicitly call it 'the opposite pattern', 'in contrast to the original results', and later 'reversed from significantly below chance to significantly above chance' — all three reversal conditions met relative to Study 1h's below-chance claim. Competing reading: if the original claim is taken as Zlatev's general 'default neglect' (chance-level selection), above-chance performance is a failure rather than a reversal. The authors present it as a demonstration that the original result is paradigm-specific rather than as a 'failed replication'.

effects.original_title: Default neglect in attempts at social influence
effects.original_authors: Zlatev, J. J.; Daniels, D. P.; Kim, H.; Neale, M. A.
effects.original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
effects.outcome: Percentage of choice architects selecting the optimal default (vs. 50% chance) in the Study 1h advice task with (dis)advantages framed in terms of switching to the new job
effects.contrast: observed optimal-default selection rate vs. 50% chance
effects.description: In Zlatev et al.'s (2017) Study 1h, choice architects choosing between default-framed pieces of advice to steer a new employee toward a target job selected the optimal default significantly less often than chance.
effects.citation_sentence: The "switch-framing" conditions were essentially identical to Zlatev et al.'s (2017) Study 1h, highlighting the advantage and drawback of the new job rather than the current job, with minor wording changes to maximize comparability to the novel stay-framing conditions.
effects.evidence: Experiment 3 Results and discussion (p. 700): "First, we again replicated Zlatev et al.'s (2017) original results when the (dis)advantages were framed in terms of switching to the new job. ... Overall, participants chose the optimal default 44.2% of the time, which was significantly less than chance, χ2(1, N = 391) = 4.95, p = .026".
effects.notes: Preregistered; Rady School pool, 440 in-lab and 339 online (pandemic) across the whole experiment. Authors call the switch conditions 'essentially identical' to Study 1h with minor wording changes -> direct (tiebreaker direct vs close -> direct); close extension is a competing type reading given partial online administration. Subgroups: higher pay 42.6% significantly below chance (p = .045), vacation 45.9% n.s. (p = .284); pooled significantly below chance and authors say 'we again replicated'. The novel stay-framing conditions of Experiment 3 (57.2%, significantly above chance) are a new manipulation to test the default-framing confound, labelled 'novel' by the authors, and are not coded as a replication entry.

effects.original_title: Default neglect in attempts at social influence
effects.original_authors: Zlatev, J. J.; Daniels, D. P.; Kim, H.; Neale, M. A.
effects.original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
effects.outcome: Percentage of choice architects selecting the optimal default (vs. 50% chance) when choosing which restaurant to propose by text message to a friend
effects.contrast: observed optimal-default selection rate vs. 50% chance
effects.description: Zlatev et al. (2017) claimed that choice architects exhibit 'default neglect', selecting the optimal default to influence others' choices at no better than chance level.
effects.citation_sentence: It is thus not entirely surprising (cf. Wilson & Wixted, 2018) that this effect does not consistently hold up in the conceptual replications reported here and elsewhere (e.g., Jung et al., 2018). When we presented participants with simple scenarios in Experiments 1A and 1B, we instead found that they were excellent at setting defaults, with performance closer to perfect optimality than chance (87.7% and 77.8% of the time, respectively).
effects.evidence: Experiment 1A Results and discussion (p. 697): "Overall, participants selected the optimal default 87.7% of the time, χ2(1, N = 146) = 81.38, p < .001, 95% CI [81.0%, 92.3%] (see Fig. 2), clearly demonstrating default sensitivity."
effects.notes: INCLUSION IS DEBATABLE: Experiments 1A/1B are new paradigms (interpersonal restaurant text message; course-enrollment policy) and are not labelled replications where they are introduced; only Experiment 2 is called a replication in the abstract/intro. Included because the General Discussion refers to 'the conceptual replications reported here' and immediately cites Experiments 1A and 1B, and because they test Zlatev et al.'s general default-neglect claim with a different procedure (same CA-chooses-default logic, cf. Jung et al. 2018 'conceptual replications'). Original claim treated as a chance-level (no-ability) claim, so significantly above-chance selection = failure; the authors frame it as contradicting default neglect. If an adjudicator judges 1A/1B to be new original experiments, drop this entry.
